name: Yusuf Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what is your normal shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am junior on plastic injection presses making small clips for car interiors, and I check the first parts for short shots and flash. I finished secondary school and still call the setter for a difficult die change. Weekend shifts pay me above the usual operator rate, even though I am learning.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like, and how do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Aylin works as a pharmacist, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. More than six months of expenses are saved, and plenty of other factories are nearby. I use AI every day to look up fault codes, then check the plastic part and press settings with the setter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the moulding crew my AI fault lookup is useful for naming a short shot, but the sample part still needs a gauge. A clean dashboard will not make a warped clip fit a car door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The plant has regular orders, and a weekend premium puts my wage above most machine operators. My partner Aylin works as a pharmacist; our two children and mortgage are covered by more than six months saved, with plenty of similar factories nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep feeding pellets, checking first moulded clips and asking the setter before changing a die. I would put extra money from each new weekend premium into the children’s savings account after the mortgage is paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, if a bit disappointed. I enjoy learning, but a plateau leaves enough good work for me to improve on the press.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is a short shot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The plastic fails to fill the last thin corner of the mould, leaving a clip that will not lock. I find it with a gauge before the bin is full.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the children’s transfer be new saving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. The six-month reserve stays where it is, and only fresh weekend pay goes into that account. I would not count the same cash twice.

say: I would tell the **moulding crew** an AI lookup still needs a physical gauge.
I would keep the **setter involved** before a die change.
think: Regular **orders and higher pay** keep our household secure.
Aylin’s wage, **strong savings** and many nearby factories give choices.
do: Feed **plastic pellets** and gauge first clips after each mould change.
Add **fresh weekend pay** to the children’s savings account.
feel: **Calm**, though modest AI progress is less interesting than I hoped.
S0.quote: A clean dashboard will not make a warped clip fit a car door.
fieldNote: Yusuf already uses an **AI fault lookup** daily, so continued use is not new learning.
He adds **fresh premium pay** to savings rather than relabelling the existing reserve.

steps.text: Keep feeding moulding presses and gauging first clips
Add new weekend premium to children’s savings after mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the plant that faster tooling plans should give operators shorter, safer shifts, not just fewer names on a rota. I would take the first trial results to the union meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI may make planning and buying quicker, and a robotic loader could eventually reduce junior shifts. I want to help set up the equipment, but a lost weekend premium would still cut what Aylin and I save for the mortgage and children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for a paid guarded practice place on new loader controls after a full-week trial, then compare defect rates with our current press. If offered the place, I would learn the controls; I would bring staffing figures to the union meeting and keep my paid shifts meanwhile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the premium and keen on a better machine. I can support automation and still insist that the people operating it get paid time to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must the trial measure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It should measure damaged clips, stops and guard breaches across a full production week. The safety lead must sign the isolation method before I touch the loader.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the union to seek?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A written paid training schedule and no silent loss of the weekend premium during practice. I would bring the actual trial figures rather than a sales sheet.

think: Robot loading could cut my **weekend premium** despite stronger production.
Aylin’s wage and **savings** help, but lost paid hours still matter.

Learn **new loader controls** if that safe place is offered.

feel: **Anxious** about premium loss, yet eager to test a safer machine.

fieldNote: His new-control practice needs an **offered place**, paid hours and signed safety isolation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI reaches tooling plans in 2028 when I am forty five, and capable mould-handling robots follow around 2031 when I am forty eight. A robot cell must prove its stop and guard before anyone removes an operator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect some junior moulding hours to disappear quickly once robots can clear jams and change tools. Our savings, Aylin’s pharmacy wage and many nearby plants give me a search window, but I cannot assume my higher weekend rate exists elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid press shift and ask for a supervised robot-cell trial on scrap parts. I would join only if the plant offers a paid guarded place; if two rosters cut my hours, I would apply only to a posted nearby moulding or robot-setting role that matches my base wage and has written safe access.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the rate and for colleagues with less saved. My own cushion lets me look carefully, not pretend the job loss has already happened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you inspect in the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the emergency stop, tool-change guard and first clip after the robot resets a fault. A qualified setter would stand with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a lower-paid robot job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after Aylin and I compare the actual wage with mortgage and school costs. A clever title cannot pay for a shortfall every month.

say: I would separate **2028 tooling AI** from hands-on robots around 2031.
I would insist on a **guarded robot trial** before junior moulding shifts change.
think: My **weekend rate** may be hard to replace if robots remove hours.
Savings, Aylin’s wage and **nearby plants** give time, not guaranteed equal pay.
do: Request a **paid supervised scrap-part trial**, joining only if offered a guarded place.
Keep **paid press shifts** while the staffing plan is unknown.
Apply after **two cut rosters** only to posted nearby comparable-base-pay roles with safe access.
feel: **Anxious** about lost rate and colleagues with weaker cushions.
S2.quote: A clever title cannot pay for a shortfall every month.
fieldNote: Yusuf requests a trial and makes **participation conditional** on an offered paid safe place.
His fallback application retains **two reduced rosters**, real local posting, comparable base pay and written access.

steps.text: Request paid supervised robot trial and join only if guarded place offered
Keep paid moulding shifts while staffing is unknown
Apply after two cut rosters to posted nearby role matching base pay with written safe access

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the union thinking AI reaches tooling plans in 2031 when I am forty eight, and capable mould-handling robots around 2034 when I am fifty one. Five years is enough to offer real paid study before a physical shift disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could qualify for maintenance, but a diploma is useful only if a plant posts a safe role at a wage we can use. My current AI lookup helps me ask better questions; it does not teach me to isolate a hot press.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would enrol in a fully funded mechatronics course if the plant offers paid workshop days and an actual practical place. After qualifying, I would apply to a posted nearby robot-maintenance job only if it covers our bills and lists isolation duties; I would also take these training terms to the union committee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about what the presses become, but I can use a real course if it exists. I would rather finish one paid qualification than collect five introductions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you practise on the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A qualified maintainer would isolate a stopped press and have me trace a failed loader sensor, then check the restart. A drawing alone would not be enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course costs your wages?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay on the paid press and ask the union to bargain for study hours. Our savings should remain a cushion for the children, not a subsidy for an employer’s training gap.

say: I would ask for **paid practical study** before 2034 mould robots spread.
I would distinguish **2031 thinking AI** from later press work.
think: A **maintenance diploma** needs a safe posted local role at adequate pay.
My existing **AI lookup** is not an isolation qualification.
do: Enrol in **funded paid-time study** only if a workshop place is offered.
Apply after **qualification** only to posted nearby bill-covering robot maintenance with written isolation duties.
Bring **training terms** to the union committee while keeping press pay.
feel: **Uneasy**, with a course and job route to verify.
S3.quote: I would rather finish one paid qualification than collect five introductions.
fieldNote: **Actual enrolment** depends on an offered funded paid workshop place.
His later **job application** needs qualification, a real local posting, adequate wages and written safety duties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the union thinking AI arrives in 2036 when I am fifty three, while capable press robots follow around 2039 when I am fifty six. A longer runway should mean paid qualifications for every shift, including nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The children may be grown, yet the mortgage and wages still matter at fifty six. Our savings buy time, and many factories are nearby, but no chart guarantees a posted maintenance job or the same premium.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep the press shift, add fresh weekend pay to the children’s account and ask the union committee for paid practical training terms. In the first year after 2036, if still employed, I would compare actual rosters and postings; after sustained cuts I would apply only to a posted local role at a household-covering wage with written safe access.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about distant press work, calmer about today’s money. Thirteen years is enough to prepare if paid places are real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a robot for yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if a paying business and a safe permitted place existed; right now I would not spend the family reserve on a forecast. I would focus on a paid qualification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask older operators?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask which shifts they could attend and which controls they want taught first. Training for older factory operators should be paid and reachable, not reserved for daytime managers.

say: I would demand **paid qualifications** for night and day crews.
I would keep **2036 thinking AI** separate from 2039 physical robots.
think: At **fifty six**, household costs may still require wages.
Savings and **nearby plants** give options without promising a matching premium.
do: Keep **press shifts** now and add fresh weekend pay to children’s savings.
Raise **paid training terms** with the union committee.
Apply after **sustained post-2036 cuts** only to posted household-covering safe local work.
feel: **Uneasy** about later press work, with current money secure.
S4.quote: Training for older factory operators should be paid and reachable, not reserved for daytime managers.
fieldNote: Yusuf separates **2026 paid work** from conditional employment and job searches after 2036.

steps.text: Keep press shift and save fresh weekend pay for children

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable robots might take junior press hours around 2031, and the weekend rate could be hard to replace. A paid guarded trial, funded practical qualification and posted local jobs with safe duties and adequate wages would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets the first paid place beside the robot when a moulding cell changes. A worker cannot learn a hot press safely in an unpaid lunch break.

headlineQuote: A worker cannot learn a hot press safely in an unpaid lunch break.
portrait: **Yusuf**, 43, is a junior injection-moulding operator with secondary schooling and daily AI fault lookup.
His **higher weekend pay**, pharmacist partner, two children, mortgage, strong savings and many local plants provide choices.
He is **adaptive** about controls and active in union meetings, while requiring guarded paid practice and written safety terms.
Fast robots threaten **junior hours**; a longer warning allows a conditional funded maintenance qualification and real job applications.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut Yusuf’s junior press hours around 2031 and make his weekend rate hard to replace.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid guarded trial**, funded practical study and posted safe local jobs at adequate wages would help.
